conceptTag: Nintendo: from playing cards to video games
readerTitle: How a playing-card maker found its way to Mario
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Nintendo, 1889~1983) + 일화 (1960년대 다각화 시도 일부) + 가상 적용 (사내 재무팀, 청소 회사)
insight: 먼 곳으로 가는 성장도 실제로는 이미 가진 것을 하나씩 이어 가는 가까운 걸음의 사다리로 이루어진다.
misconception: 성장이 멈추면 아무 데나 빠르게 크는 시장으로 뛰어들어 위험을 분산하는 것이 안전하다.

sources.text: Nintendo Co., Ltd., corporate history (1889 founding, hanafuda cards, 1959 Disney character cards, Ultra Hand, Game & Watch, Family Computer)
Sheff, D. (1993). Game Over: How Nintendo Conquered the World. Random House. (1960년대 다각화 시도: 택시, 즉석밥 등, Gunpei Yokoi와 Ultra Hand)
Nintendo 'Iwata Asks' interview series and Gunpei Yokoi profiles (Ultra Hand origin)

factChecks.note: 1889년 교토에서 Fusajiro Yamauchi가 화투(hanafuda)로 창업, 1959년 Disney 캐릭터 카드 출시, 1966년 Ultra Hand, 1980년 Game & Watch, 1983년 일본 Famicom 출시. 게시 전에 Nintendo 공식 연혁으로 연도를 다시 확인하세요.
1960년대 택시 회사, 즉석밥 사업은 Sheff(1993) 등 여러 자료에 나옵니다. 러브호텔 운영설은 출처가 약해 카드에서 'reportedly'로 표시했습니다. 각 사업의 정확한 손실 규모는 쓰지 않았습니다.
1960년대 중반 카드 수요가 정점을 지나 꺾였다는 서술은 정성적으로만 썼습니다. 구체적 판매·주가 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.
Gunpei Yokoi가 설비 유지보수 담당이었고 여가 시간에 만든 장난감이 Ultra Hand가 되었다는 이야기는 널리 전해지지만 세부 내용은 자료마다 다릅니다. 카드에서 'the story goes'로 표시했습니다.
Nintendo가 오늘날에도 화투와 카드를 판매한다는 내용을 게시 직전에 공식 사이트로 확인하세요.

cards.title: How a playing-card maker found its way to Mario
body: In 1889, a small shop in Kyoto began making *hanafuda*, Japanese flower-patterned playing cards. The shop was called Nintendo.
Nearly a century later, the same company launched one of the best-selling home video game consoles. Along the way, it also tried taxis and instant rice.

image.label: A hanafuda card turning into a game controller
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 꽃 그림 화투 한 장, 오른쪽으로 갈수록 장난감, 휴대용 게임기, 게임 컨트롤러로 단계적으로 변해 가는 모습. 실제 Nintendo 로고, 캐릭터, 제품 디자인은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Card sales have peaked. Where do you grow?
body: It's the mid-1960s. You run Japan's leading playing-card maker. Cards with Disney characters were a hit, but demand is now falling.
You have cash, factories, a known brand and a few clever engineers. What's your next move?

options.text: Enter fast-growing industries like taxis and packaged food to spread the risk
options.feedback: You get new markets quickly, but you bring nothing they need. You compete as a beginner against experts.

options.text: Move into toys and games, building on what you know about making things people play with
options.feedback: It's still a new market, but your skills, brand and sense of play carry over. You give up some speed for a real head start.

options.text: Stay with cards: cut costs and sign more character licenses
options.feedback: Safe and familiar, and it buys time. But a shrinking market caps how far you can grow.

cards.title: Nintendo tried almost everything.
body: Under president Hiroshi Yamauchi, Nintendo tried A and B at once. It started a taxi company, sold instant rice and, reportedly, ran a short-stay hotel. These bets went nowhere.
Meanwhile, the story goes, a maintenance engineer named Gunpei Yokoi built an extending grabber arm for fun. Yamauchi had it sold as a toy. The **Ultra Hand** became a hit in 1966.
Toys led to light-gun games, then electronic games. Cards, not taxis, pointed the way.

cards.title: Related diversification
body: **Related diversification** means entering a new business that shares something real with the one you have: customers, skills, channels or brand.
Taxis and rice shared nothing with cards. Toys shared a lot: the same promise of fun, the same families buying, and a team that knew how to design for play.
The further a move is from what you already do well, the more you must learn from scratch, and the more rivals know than you.

cards.title: No single step was a giant leap.
body: Looking back, cards to consoles seems huge. Each step was close to the last one.

breakdown.label: Ultra Hand
breakdown.detail: A toy for the same families

cards.softwareNote: Software companies grow the same way. A tool for one task adds the next task the same users do, then sells to their neighbors in the company. Each feature borrows trust from the last.

cards.title: Teams inside a company face the same choice.
body: A finance team builds excellent monthly reports. Leadership offers it a bigger role: run office purchasing, or build reports for sales and operations.
Purchasing is a bigger budget, but it needs supplier skills the team lacks. Reports for other departments reuse its data skills and earn trust with new internal customers.
The second move looks smaller. It's the one the team can win.

cards.title: Hindsight makes the ladder look obvious.
body: Nintendo didn't follow a neat plan. It ran several bets, and only the related ones worked. That still cost money and years.
Talent and timing mattered too. Without Yokoi, the toy step might have stalled.
And relatedness isn't magic. A move can share your customers and still fail if the product is weak. Use closeness to rank options, not to skip testing them.

image.label: Several paths branching, only one climbing upward
image.brief: 갈림길 일러스트. 여러 갈래 길 중 택시, 밥그릇 아이콘이 있는 길은 끊겨 있고, 장난감 아이콘이 있는 길만 계단처럼 위로 이어짐. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Now it's a home cleaning company.
body: Your cleaning business has loyal weekly clients, trusted staff and a booking system. Growth has slowed. Which next step builds on what you have?

options.text: Open a café, since the neighborhood lacks one
options.feedback: A real opportunity, maybe. But none of your clients, skills or systems help you run a café.

options.text: Offer deep cleans, windows and move-out cleaning to current clients
options.feedback: Same clients, same staff, same booking system. Growth is slower than a big leap, but you start with every advantage.

options.text: Start a staffing agency supplying cleaners to hotels
options.feedback: Your hiring skills carry over, but hotels are new customers with different buying habits. It could be a later rung on the ladder.

cards.title: Grow by the next rung, not the farthest jump.
body: Nintendo reached video games through steps that each shared something with the last. Its unrelated leaps went nowhere.
**Try it today:** list three growth ideas. For each, write what it shares with your business today: customers, skills, channels or brand. Rank them by that list.
